opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Raj, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay, but I only have twenty minutes, I'm due back at the shop. I own two convenience stores. I work most hours God sends, so be quick with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good. I use it sometimes for the supplier emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing. My problem isn't emails. My problem is finding someone reliable for the night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Same seventy hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Normal. Tired, but that's not the AI.

S0.say: Fine, good. I use it sometimes for supplier emails.
S0.think: It changes nothing. My real problem is finding someone reliable for the night shift.
S0.do: Carries on with the same seventy-hour weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort it out. It always does if government stays out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow is fine for me. Maybe the ordering software gets smarter and saves me an hour a week. That's an hour with my kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try one of the stock ordering apps for one store first, see if it cuts waste. If it works, both stores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little hopeful.

S1.say: The market will sort it out if government stays out.
S1.think: Smarter ordering software might save me an hour a week. That's an hour with my kids.
S1.do: Trials a stock ordering app in one store, then rolls it out to both if it cuts waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office people have had it easy for a long time. Now they know how a shopkeeper feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, more people looking for work means I can finally find good night staff. But if my customers lose their jobs, they spend less on coffee and cigarettes and lottery tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hire a better night manager while people are available, and I'd watch my takings week by week. I'd cut stock of the expensive lines first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. One eye on the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd say office people had it easy. Is that something you'd really say out loud, in the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the shop, no, never. They're my customers. At home, with family, yes.

S2.say: Office people have had it easy. Now they know how a shopkeeper feels.
S2.think: I'd only say that at home, never in the shop. More jobseekers means good night staff, but customers who lose jobs will spend less.
S2.do: Hires a better night manager while people are available, tracks takings weekly and cuts back on expensive lines.
S2.feel: Mostly fine, one eye on the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government will use this crisis to tax small business to death. Watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shops sell to people. If lots of people lose good jobs, they still buy milk, but they stop buying the extras where I make my money. And a political crisis means new taxes. That's always where it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go through every cost line, renegotiate with suppliers and cut my own pay first. I'd hold off on the third store I was thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've been through bad times before. I know how to tighten.

S3.say: The government will use this crisis to tax small business to death.
S3.think: People still buy milk but stop buying the extras where I make my money. And new taxes always land on me.
S3.do: Goes through every cost, renegotiates with suppliers, cuts his own pay first and shelves plans for a third store.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but he knows how to tighten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say about time. Let a robot stack shelves at 3 a.m. and let me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is what I've wanted for years. But the big chains get the robots first, cheaper, and then their prices fall and mine don't. If I can afford one robot for the night shift, I'm saved. If I can't, I'm finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find out the price on day one. I'd ask the bank about a loan, or a lease, like with the fridges. I'd rather owe money on a robot than lose to the supermarket down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and worried at the same time. Like a big bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your staff do the work a robot would do. Have you thought about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd keep my day staff, they know the customers. The night shift, I'm sorry, but nobody wants that shift anyway. I've been doing it myself.

S4.say: About time. Let a robot stack shelves at 3 a.m. and let me sleep.
S4.think: The chains get robots first and cheaper. If I can afford one for the night shift, I'm saved. If not, I'm finished.
S4.do: Gets prices on day one, asks the bank about a loan or lease, and plans to keep day staff while automating the night shift.
S4.feel: Hopeful and worried, like a big bet.
